what’s the matter? phrase

also what’s wrong?, what’s wrong with you?, what’s up?, what ails you?, what on earth’s the matter?, what is it?, what’s the trouble now?, what’s it all about?

classical

Traupman 92
Traupman 409: what’s wrong with you?, quid est tibi? or quid est tēcum?
Plaut. Curc. 236: sed quid tibi est?
Traupman 55
Traupman 61
Traupman 62: what ails you?

Quid tibi est?

Other words

  • Quid reī est? — what’s up? what’s going on?

    also used · modern · Traupman 111

    Literally “what of a matter is it?”. Not found in Lewis & Short or the loci collections in this form; Traupman is the only evidence.

  • Quid est? — what is it? what’s the matter?

    also used · classical · Ter. And. 184: Hem, quid est?; Traupman 103: quid est?; Traupman 115

    The plain answer to being called or to a worried face; Quid tibi est? asks what is wrong with the person.

  • Quidnam est? — what on earth is it?

    also used · classical · Ter. Ad. 537–538; Traupman 103: what on earth’s the matter?, quidnam est?

    -nam makes the question urgent or surprised.

  • Quid istuc est reī? — what’s the matter (with that)?

    also used · classical · Traupman 103: quid istuc est reī?; Liv. 3.48.4: quid hoc reī sit (Lewis & Short s.v. percontor)

    The partitive genitive reī with a neuter pronoun, as Livy asks quid hoc reī sit, “what this is all about”; Plautus builds quid istuc est verbī? the same way (Plaut. Curc. 1.1.32). The exact words are Traupman’s.

  • Quid jam? — given for “what (is the trouble) now?”

    avoid · classical · Traupman 111

    In Plautus quid jam? is “why so? how so?” and is answered with quia (Plaut. Mil. 2.3.51, Lewis & Short s.v. luscitiōsus; see why so?). For what is wrong, Quid tibi est? (above) or Quid istuc malī est? (see trouble).

Examples

  • «Quid tibi est? Aurēs dolent?»

    “What’s the matter? Do your ears hurt?”Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam

  • quid agis? — Vīvō. — Nempe ut dignus es. sed quid tibi est?

    How are you? — Alive. — As you deserve, no doubt. But what’s wrong with you?Plaut. Curc. 235–236

  • Dāve. — Hem, quid est? — Ehodum ad mē!

    Davus! — Eh, what is it? — Come here to me!Ter. And. 184

  • Hem tibi autem. — Quidnam est? — Lupus in fābulā.

    Look out! — What on earth is it? — Speak of the devil.Ter. Ad. 537–538

See also why so sad?, what happened?, why so?, trouble.
